notes.meaning: God is pictured arriving in majesty on a swift cloud to bring judgment to Egypt. The false gods of the land shake in fear before Him because they cannot protect their people. The courage of the Egyptians melts away when they see that the true Lord has arrived.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Ancient Christian writers such as Jerome believed this was fulfilled when the child Jesus was taken to Egypt and the pagan statues fell to the ground.

notes.meaning: The Lord causes the people of Egypt to turn against each other in civil war. Brothers, neighbors, and rival cities fight among themselves instead of standing together. God uses their own internal fighting to bring down the nation.

Egypt was famous for ancient wisdom, but God empties out their good judgment. In desperation and panic, the people consult idols, ghosts, and fortune-tellers. None of these dark arts can rescue them from the Lord.
God hands the Egyptians over to harsh and cruel masters. A ruthless king will rule over them with an iron fist. Because they lost their wisdom and unity, they fall into bitter slavery.

The great Nile River, which looks like a wide sea to the people, begins to dry up. Egypt depended completely on the regular rising of the river to water its crops. When the riverbed is left parched, the whole country faces terrible famine.

The irrigation canals become stagnant and smell bad as the water trickles away. The plants that grow along the water, like reeds and rushes, dry up and die. The water channels that once shielded the country from attackers can no longer defend it.

The rich pastures and planted fields along the banks of the Nile wither into dust. Strong winds blow the dried-up crops away until nothing remains. Without the river, the fertile farm country turns into barren desert.

The fishermen who make their living on the Nile weep and mourn because their work is gone. Both those who fish with hooks in the canals and those who spread nets in the river find nothing. The common food supply that everyone relied on is wiped out.

The craftspeople who comb fine flax and weave expensive linen are stunned and disappointed. Egypt was famous across the ancient world for making fine cloth for priests and kings. When the plants fail, this entire trade collapses.

The leaders who support society are brought low, and ordinary workers are deeply discouraged. People who build fishponds or work for daily wages lose their living. The economic ruin touches every level of society.

The royal officials in the famous city of Zoan act like fools. They brag about coming from wise families and ancient kings, yet they give senseless advice to Pharaoh. Human wisdom without God fails completely in a crisis.

Pharaoh is challenged to bring out his famous wise men and magicians. If they are truly clever, they should be able to explain what the Lord of hosts has planned against Egypt. Human cleverness cannot discover what God has decided.

The rulers in Zoan and Memphis are completely deceived by their own pride. These princes were supposed to be the cornerstones holding up the tribes of the nation, but they lead the country straight into disaster. When rulers trust in themselves, their people suffer.

The Lord pours a spirit of deep confusion into the leaders of Egypt. Because they turned away from God, they make foolish choices and stumble in everything they do. They wander around helplessly like a drunk person falling in his own vomit.

There is nothing anyone in Egypt can do to fix their trouble. Neither the powerful leaders at the top nor the ordinary laborers at the bottom can stop the disaster. When God brings judgment, every human scheme fails.

The Egyptians will lose their fighting courage and panic like helpless people. They will tremble when they realize that the Lord of hosts is raising His hand against them. No nation can stand against the mighty power of God.

The name of little Judah will strike dread into the hearts of the Egyptians. Egypt used to look down on Judah, but now they fear the God of Judah and what He has decreed. Remembering what the Lord is doing makes their hearts shake.

God promises that a remnant of Egyptian cities will turn to worship Him. They will speak the language of Canaan, which means they will agree with God's people and confess the true faith. Even a city once famous for sun worship will give its loyalty to the Lord.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars read the Hebrew title as City of Destruction, understanding it as a wordplay on the tearing down of Egyptian idols.

notes.meaning: True worship will be set up openly in the middle of Egypt and marked at its border. An altar shows that they worship the Lord, and a stone pillar marks their land as dedicated to Him. This points forward to the day when people outside Israel worship God from the heart.

differ.view: Reformed Christians take the altar as a symbol of spiritual Christian worship, prayer, and praise rather than a physical altar for animal sacrifices.
Some evangelicals believe a physical altar will literally be built in Egypt during a future thousand-year earthly reign of Christ.

notes.meaning: The altar and pillar will show the world that Egypt belongs to the Lord of hosts. When the people face cruel oppressors and cry out to God, He will send a mighty Savior to rescue them. God shows the same tender mercy to repenting Gentiles that He showed to Israel in the past.

differ.view: Reformed Christians believe the Savior sent to rescue them is Jesus Christ delivering people from sin and the devil.
Many evangelicals understand the savior historically as an earthly conqueror such as Alexander the Great who freed Egypt from Persian rule.

notes.meaning: The Lord will reveal Himself to Egypt, and the people will truly know Him. They will offer sincere worship and make solemn promises to serve Him faithfully. True faith always leads people to love God and keep their word to Him.

The Lord will strike Egypt with painful troubles, but His real goal is to heal them. When His discipline leads them to repent and pray, He will listen and restore them. God uses hard times to turn our hearts back to Himself.

A broad highway will connect Egypt and Assyria, two old enemies who fought each other for generations. The people of both nations will travel freely to visit one another, and they will worship the true God side by side. The gospel breaks down old hatreds and unites former enemies in peaceful worship.

Israel will join together with Egypt and Assyria in a shared bond of faith. These three lands, which once lived in endless conflict, will become a blessing to the whole earth. God uses His redeemed people to bring peace and light to surrounding nations.

The Lord speaks words of special love over all three nations together. He calls Egypt His people, Assyria His handiwork, and Israel His prized inheritance. In Christ, God welcomes people from every background into one family of faith.
